reconcile.connective: Commentators distinguish two senses of perfection: the law was morally blameless, as the psalm says, yet inadequate on its own to save, as Hebrews argues.

discrepancy.connective: Isaac Troki presses the reverse case: he rebuts Hebrews' claim that the old covenant 'waxeth old' by citing scripture affirming God's ordinances stand forever.

skeptic.name: Isaac Troki
skeptic.attribution: Isaac Troki (d. 1594), Chizzuk Emunah / Faith Strengthened (1593; Eng. trans. Mocatta, 1851)

excerpts.excerpt_text: The law in its morality was blameless (Greek, "amomos"); but in saving us it was defective, and so not faultless (Greek, "amemptos").
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly answers the perfect-vs-faultless tension by distinguishing the law's moral blamelessness (matching Ps 19:7's temimah) from its salvific inadequacy (matching Heb 8:7's amemptos) — two different predicates, not a flat contradiction.

pd_work.resource: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-1763)
pd_work.author: John Gill
pd_work.note: Gill comments on both Psalm 19:7 and Hebrews 8:7 directly (not merely the general topic): he argues the 'perfect' law-language of the psalm fits the gospel/doctrine of the Lord better than the Mosaic law, and that the old covenant's 'not faultless' meant deficient in application, not sinful in itself — the harmonizing move Haley's index does not separately cover for this exact pairing.
